terms.gloss: to name a day for someone’s trial, to summon or impeach him
evidence: Cic. Mil. 36: diem mihi, crēdō, dīxerat (Lewis & Short s.v. diēs)
terms.comment: Latin says it with a verb: the magistrate names the day. We have found no noun for a summons in the reference works; Traupman too gives only “serve a summons on”.

terms.gloss: to serve a summons on someone
terms.comment: Traupman’s phrase. We have found no classical instance of diem dare in this sense; the classical phrase is diem dīcere.

evidence: Cic. Quinct. 61: in jūs vocās: sequitur (Lewis & Short s.v. vocō)
terms.comment: The plaintiff’s summons in private law: the defendant had to follow him before the magistrate (see court).

terms.gloss: set in quick motion, rouse; call, summon (the senate, the judges, a party to a suit)
evidence: Liv. 1.47.8: patrēs in cūriam per praecōnem ad rēgem Tarquinium citārī jussit (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Verr. 2.1.19: jūdicēs citātī in hunc reum cōnsēdistis (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: patrēs in cūriam per praecōnem ad rēgem Tarquinium citārī jussit
phrases.english: he ordered the senators to be summoned by a herald to the senate-house, to King Tarquin

sources: Lewis & Short: dies · Lewis & Short: voco
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 196.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
